name: Nonspecific low back pain

diagnosisContested.note: The label itself is not seriously disputed, but it is a diagnosis of exclusion: WHO defines chronic primary low back pain as pain lasting more than 3 months that is not due to an underlying disease or other condition. It covers a mixed population, and it presumes serious pathology has been ruled out, which an app cannot do. The guideline's movement control impairment subgroup is a clinician classification and cannot be self-assigned in an app (expert opinion, this review).

avoidOrModify.movement: Prolonged bed rest or stopping ordinary activity because of back pain
avoidOrModify.rationale: Advice to stay active gave small improvements over advice to rest in bed for acute low back pain (2 trials, N = 401: pain SMD 0.22, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.41; function SMD 0.29, 0.09 to 0.49; moderate quality). For sciatica there was little or no difference, so this is weaker with leg symptoms. Advice to stay active alone has little benefit, but there is no evidence of harm from it and potential harm from prolonged bed rest. NICE recommends encouraging normal activities, and the George guideline retains text against education promoting extended bed rest. The Dahm search ended in May 2009.

avoidOrModify.movement: Lumbar flexion (rounding the lower back) while lifting, only where it provokes the person's symptoms
avoidOrModify.rationale: Do not apply this as a blanket ban. Low-quality evidence found greater lumbar flexion during lifting is not a risk factor for onset or persistence (peak flexion difference 1.5 degrees, -0.7 to 3.7, longitudinal). An umbrella review of 41 reviews found no consensus on causality for bending or lifting. Against that, occupational lifting/carrying (OR 1.7, 1.4 to 2.2) and non-neutral postures (OR 1.5, 1.2 to 1.9) are associated with chronic pain, which is association from highest-versus-lowest work exposure and not evidence on gym loading. In a modelling study stoop lifting had lower compression but higher shear than squat lifting, so neither style is simply safe. The modify rule itself rests on individual symptom response (expert opinion).

avoidOrModify.movement: Loaded spinal flexion or lifting in a person with known osteoporosis, long-term corticosteroid use or previous spinal fracture
avoidOrModify.rationale: A secondary summary of the IFOMPT framework describes spinal fracture as often following a fall or lifting in flexion, with these as risk factors. Applying that to exercise selection is an inference, not a tested rule. Such users should get clinician clearance.

avoidOrModify.movement: Heavy spinal loading during a flare, such as heavily loaded hinges or squats, or heavy deadlifting with high current pain or low back-extensor endurance
avoidOrModify.rationale: Not a prohibition. Supervised heavy deadlifting was neither better nor worse than low-load motor control on pain and disability at 2, 12 or 24 months. But within the deadlift arm, higher pain, more disability and poorer Biering-Sorensen endurance predicted less benefit, and the authors advise sufficient back-extensor capacity and a low enough pain level first. That trial progressed training if pain had not increased. In one loaded-training trial, a transient flare-up in each group was managed by temporarily reducing load or repetitions. The prediction models are small and not validated, and no source gives a safe load limit. Fatigue protocols increased trunk range of motion, and higher load increased spinal flexion, in studies cited by a narrative review. Extending the deadlift findings to hinges and squats is an inference.

avoidOrModify.movement: Using stretching as the entire exercise programme
avoidOrModify.rationale: Stretching is not contraindicated, but it did not differ from true control for pain or function in one network meta-analysis, was the one type not beating control for pain in another, and showed no effect on disability in older adults (MD -0.3, -9.53 to 8.93). Specific trunk activation outperformed stretching in small trials in a movement control impairment subgroup. Contrary evidence exists: flexibility exercise had a moderate-to-important function effect in Hayden 2021 NMA and hamstring stretching reduced pain in Gou 2024 (SMD -0.72, I2 89%). Combine it with strengthening or general exercise.

avoidOrModify.movement: Exercise that keeps worsening the pain, or progressing load while pain is rising
avoidOrModify.rationale: Re-added on new sources. A deadlift trial progressed training if pain had not increased. A narrative review reports the Canadian guideline rule: when exercise exacerbates pain, have a physical therapist assess the programme, and if it still does, a physician assess the patient. Pain alone need not stop exercise: KNGF advises time-contingent rather than pain-contingent build-up, and accepts increased pain of short duration (part of a day) with moderately irritable radicular syndrome. One trial reported transient soreness under 24 hours. No trial tested a pain threshold.

avoidOrModify.movement: High-intensity Pilates when low intensity is available
avoidOrModify.rationale: In a 168-person trial higher intensity added no pain or disability benefit but more side effects (absolute risk reduction with low intensity 0.20, 0.10 to 0.31). Authors recommend low intensity. The abstract does not define intensity or adverse event types, and the result applies to clinical Pilates only.

avoidOrModify.movement: Deliberate abdominal contraction as a constant cue during Pilates
avoidOrModify.rationale: Cueing a relaxed abdomen beat cueing core contraction on disability by a slight amount (-1.4 on a 0-24 scale, -2.6 to -0.2), not clearly on pain (-0.6, -1.4 to 0.2). One trial, abstract only, and it does not address bracing under heavy load.

avoidOrModify.movement: End-range spinal flexion or extension in Pilates or yoga
avoidOrModify.rationale: A national consensus says patients 'should avoid excessive spinal flexion or extension movements' in Pilates and yoga; this is advice and not a trial result, and it sits uneasily with the lifting-flexion evidence above. Yoga carried more adverse events than no exercise at 6-12 months, primarily increased back pain (RR 4.76, 2.08 to 10.89; 43 vs 9 per 1000; low certainty), though not more than other exercise (RR 0.93, 0.56 to 1.53).

avoidOrModify.movement: Relying on a lumbar belt, brace or corset as treatment
avoidOrModify.rationale: NICE says do not offer belts or corsets; the WHO summary lists lumbar braces, belts and supports as not for routine care (very low certainty). Back belts did not prevent episodes (RR 1.01, 0.71 to 1.44). These sources address treatment and prevention, and none addresses a lifting belt worn for heavy strength training. Not a movement property, so it needs an education or rule mechanism.

dose.notes: Start at 10 kg including bar. Rest 5 min (Tataryn table only; Michaelson states no rest). candidateExercises.cautions: WalkBack enrolled people recently recovered from pain and measured recurrence (HR 0.72, 0.60 to 0.85), so it is not a treatment dose for current pain. redFlags.sign: With back or leg pain: new or worsening trouble starting or maintaining urination, or not emptying the bladder
redFlags.action: Stop and seek emergency help immediately; possible cauda equina syndrome.

redFlags.sign: With back or leg pain: new or worsening loss of bowel control or of the sensation of needing to pass stool
redFlags.action: Stop and seek emergency help immediately; possible cauda equina syndrome.

redFlags.sign: New or worsening altered feeling around the buttocks, genitals or between the legs
redFlags.action: Stop and seek emergency help immediately; possible cauda equina syndrome.

redFlags.sign: New or worsening changes in sexual sensation or function, with back or leg pain
redFlags.action: Stop and seek emergency help immediately; possible cauda equina syndrome.

redFlags.sign: New or worsening severe pain in both legs, or rapidly progressive leg weakness
redFlags.action: Stop and seek emergency help immediately; possible cauda equina syndrome or other serious nerve involvement.

redFlags.sign: Back pain after significant trauma, or severe localised pain with osteoporosis, long-term corticosteroid use or previous spinal fracture
redFlags.action: Stop exercising and get prompt medical assessment for possible fracture. The urgency wording is expert opinion, since the opened summaries set no timeframe.

redFlags.sign: Back pain with a past history of cancer, unexplained weight loss or night pain
redFlags.action: Stop exercising and get prompt medical assessment for possible malignancy. The urgency wording is expert opinion, since the opened summaries set no timeframe.

redFlags.sign: Back pain with fever, immunosuppression, injection-drug use, recent infection or a recent spinal procedure. Absence of fever does not exclude infection.
redFlags.action: Stop exercising and seek urgent medical assessment for possible spinal infection.

limitations: The moderate grade is narrow. It covers short-term pain versus no treatment, usual care or placebo in chronic pain (Hayden 2021, searches to April 2018). Function fell short of the review threshold, benefits fade (Verville 2023: intermediate pain SMD -0.08, -0.29 to 0.13) and no treatment reached clinical significance long term (Belavy 2026). No established dose. Every dose in this file describes what a trial did or what a model predicted. Arora 2026 states the evidence does not support a single optimal dose, and 84% of its trials were at high risk of bias. No guideline read gives a numeric prescription. Exercises were tested inside programmes. No trial here isolates the effect of plank, bird dog, dead bug, bridge or cat-cow. Exercise-level doses come mainly from Park 2026 (pilot in men) and Kshirsagar 2026 (non-randomised, young male runners), so transfer to other people is untested. Home delivery is a real gap for this app. Programme supervision beat home-only exercise in Hayden 2005 strategies and Quentin 2021, and Nicol 2023 reports insufficient evidence that home programmes differ from no care. Most deadlift evidence is supervised. Harms are under-reported. Adverse events appeared in 28.5% of trials in Arora 2026 and under 31% of reviews in Comachio 2025. IJzelenberg 2023 could reach no conclusion on safety in acute pain. In Hayden 2021, the median was 0.14 events per participant vs 0.12, mostly minor. Verville 2023 reported mixed-exercise harms OR 4.24 (0.69 to 25.95, 2 RCTs, very low certainty). Biomechanics are not outcomes. Load figures in Rezaei 2026, McGill 2012 and von Arx 2021, disc changes in Yanagisawa 2021 and flexion changes in Shoji 2025 come from healthy or trained people and set no safe limit. McGowen 2024 used body weight only, so its title should not be generalized to loaded lifts. The landmark Wilke and Callaghan load papers and powerlifting injury epidemiology were not retrieved. Implausible effects were not used. Pourahmadi 2019 (disability SMD -8.03) and the large effects in Tan 2026 and Rodriguez-Dominguez 2026 did not inform doses or claims. Access limits. Many records are abstract only, and long reviews were read in part (see each reference). WHO 2023 summary is a summary, since the full WHO guideline could not be retrieved, and all WHO recommendations are conditional (Briggs 2025). The original VA/DoD guideline was not read, so VA/DoD synopsis (Macedo 2024) and AAFP 2023 summary stand in and no grades are reported. Skelly 2026 recommendations are known only from Managed Healthcare Executive 2026. Oliveira 2026 content is unread. Nothing can be said about AAOS, because no search targeted it. Red flags are still partly secondary. Non-emergency flags rest on POGO Physio summary and iatroX VA/DoD summary, and their urgency wording is partly expert opinion. Finucane 2020 notes most red flags lack strong diagnostic accuracy evidence. Alshanqity 2025 is one case and cannot show causation or incidence. Owen 2020 notice records an expression of concern on Owen 2020, rescinded by a journal editorial note dated 27 July 2020. Screening. The movement control impairment subgroup is a clinician classification and cannot be self-assigned. The app cannot screen for serious pathology, and this is general information, not treatment. Contradictions: (1) Stretching. Owen 2020 (no difference from true control, p>0.095) and Fernandez-Rodriguez 2022 (only type not beating control for pain) against Hayden 2021 NMA (flexibility important for function), Hayden 2005 strategies (stretching and strengthening largest gains) and Gou 2024 (hamstring stretching SMD -0.72, I2 89%). Quentin 2021 also favours stretching, on pre-post effects. (2) McKenzie. Hayden 2021 NMA found moderate to important effects, and Hennemann 2025 found short-term benefit in people with a directional preference (lead author is a McKenzie Institute instructor). Owen 2020 and Fernandez-Rodriguez 2022 did not, and Almeida 2023 concluded it is not effective for (sub)acute pain. Halliday 2016 found no difference from motor control. Gao 2026 still grades it strong. (3) Dose frequency and length. Arora 2026 (3-4/week, 25-30 min, 8-13 weeks, limited benefit at higher exposure) against Wang L 2026 (6-7/week, 15-20 min, 16+ weeks), Fernandez-Rodriguez 2022 (1-2/week, 3-9 weeks), Zhang 2023 (60+ min suggested in older adults, while under-60 had a larger VAS estimate) and Kell 2011 (4 days/week best). Liang 2024 reports a U-shape. Hayden 2005 strategies found no clear dose effect. (4) Acute pain. IJzelenberg 2023, Karlsson 2020 and KNGF guideline (Apeldoorn 2024) found no clinically relevant benefit; Gianola 2022 found SMD -1.40 (-2.41 to -0.40) at immediate term against inert therapy. Qaseem 2017 and Wang XQ 2024 do not name exercise for acute pain, while George 2021 gives it can/C and Stochkendahl 2018 suggests supervised exercise if treatment is needed. Zhou 2024 counts 9 of 13 guidelines recommending it. (5) Aerobic exercise. George 2021 grades it should/A and Verville 2023 found a pain signal (very low certainty), but Searle 2015 calls cardiorespiratory programmes ineffective and Kell 2009 saw no significant improvement. No completed Cochrane review surfaced, only de Zoete 2024. (6) Core and motor control. George 2021 gives should/A to specific trunk activation; Gao 2026 only weakly recommends core stabilization; Saragiotto 2016 and KNGF guideline (Apeldoorn 2024) find it no better than other exercise. Macedo 2016 is null for acute pain. Wang XQ 2024 allows it for subacute pain. (7) Bracing. Effective protocols used bracing (Michaelson 2016, Park 2026), while Lunkes 2026 found relaxed cueing slightly better in Pilates. (8) Pilates ranking. Network analyses rank it top (Owen 2020, Fernandez-Rodriguez 2022, Liang 2024), but Yamato 2015 found no conclusive superiority over other exercise (short-term disability MD -3.29, -6.82 to 0.24) and Gao 2026 grades it weak. Tottoli 2024 found its advantage over home exercise not clinically relevant. (9) Yoga size. Li 2023 gives SMD -1.76 for pain, far above Wieland 2022 (MD -4.53/100, clinically unimportant). AAFP 2023 summary reports that yoga does not improve outcomes more than physical therapy or strength training. (10) Mind-body and aquatic. Gao 2026 strongly recommends aquatic exercise, tai chi and qigong, yet Verville 2023 found no low or unclear risk-of-bias trial for them. Li 2023 ranks tai chi highly with a wide interval. (11) Resistance size. Rodriguez-Dominguez 2026 (pain SMD -1.15, disability -2.76, GRADE moderate) against Ranzani 2025 (small, fragile), Verville 2023 (strength training immediate pain MD -0.39, -1.16 to 0.38) and Tomschi 2026 (no added benefit from one session a week). (12) Prevention. Comachio 2025 reports short-term RR 0.67 but long-term RR 1.04 (0.73 to 1.49), and no added benefit from high leisure activity. The 0.67 short-term figure matches Shiri 2018, so the two may not be independent. (13) Certainty of the headline claim. Hayden 2021 and Verville 2023 rate pain effects moderate certainty. Belavy 2026, with 551 studies, rates comparisons low (1.4%) to very low (98.6%). Innocenti 2023 shows outcome-measurement bias may slightly overestimate function effects. (14) Deadlift set and rep reporting. Michaelson 2016 gives no exact sets or reps; Tataryn 2021 tabulates 5+ x 1-10 for the same trial population. The primary Aasa 2015 report was abstract only, so this is unresolved. Michaelson 2016, Aasa 2015, Berglund 2015 and Berglund 2018 share a trial population and count as one trial. (15) Non-exercise conflicts, recorded only. Acupuncture or needling: NICE NG59 and Stochkendahl 2018 against, WHO 2023 summary and Qaseem 2017 for. NSAIDs: Stochkendahl 2018 against, Qaseem 2017 and WHO 2023 summary for. Aldera 2026 keeps the psychological-package wording that NICE NG59 removed in July 2026.
evidenceGradeNote: Moderate applies only to short-term pain with exercise versus no treatment, usual care or placebo in chronic nonspecific low back pain. Very low to low for dose, single exercises and acute pain. A 2026 time-course network meta-analysis rated nearly all comparisons very low, so this grade is at the upper end of what the evidence allows.

valuesCorrected: Plank and side plank: the 30 s and 60 s holds were knee-supported in Kshirsagar 2026 Table 1, with feet-supported work as a later progression. Asik 2025 added as the source naming forearm plank.
Barbell deadlift loads: 100 kg and 53 kg are the mean highest load lifted, not an average training load.
Verville 2023 harms OR 4.24 applies to mixed exercise in 2 RCTs, not to pooled exercise.
Ranzani 2025 flare-up management: one trial (one flare-up per group), not several trials.
Cherni 2026: fatigue protocols increased trunk range of motion; higher load increased spinal flexion.
Michaelson 2016 no-difference statement limited to pain and disability, because Aasa 2015 favoured motor control on activity at 2 months.
WalkBack starting frequency: the protocol text states it, so the note saying it came only from an unread supplement was wrong.
Macedo 2016: no benefit over other treatments and no firm conclusions from three small trials, replacing 'no clinically important benefit'.
Stock 2022: pain was mild-to-moderate, not only mild.
Berglund 2018: no change at group level; subgroups did change.
Thoracic elevation: the paper gives 'hands straight at the front'.
